lesson_title: The Day Time Became a Machine
hook_text: In 1750 a weaver started work when he felt like it. In 1830 a bell rang at six, and if you were late, you paid for it.
clip_script: Picture a cotton mill in Manchester in 1830. A steam engine in the basement burns coal and turns iron shafts that drive hundreds of machines on every floor. One worker now spins more thread than a whole village could by hand. That is the Industrial Revolution: machines, steam, factories and railways, all pushing each other forward. But look at the people. Families who lost their land poured into towns. Manchester grew from twenty-five thousand people to over three hundred thousand. In 1851 Britain became the first country where most people lived in towns. And time changed. The factory bell rang at six. The machines set the pace. Fourteen-hour days, six days a week, with fines for being late. A new middle class grew rich. A new working class owned nothing but their labour. Better life eventually came, but the first workers paid for it.
visual_style: A whiteboard cross-section of a mill with a steam engine turning shafts, a clock and bell above the door, a line graph of Manchester's population shooting upwards, and a split figure of a factory owner and a worker.
pacing: Big machine energy first, then a slower turn to the people and the clock.
